blocks.title: The atom and its isotopes
blocks.md:
An atom has a small, dense **nucleus** of protons (relative mass 1, charge +1) and neutrons (mass 1, charge 0) surrounded by electrons (mass about 1/1836, charge −1). The **atomic number** Z = number of protons; the **mass number** A = protons + neutrons.

**Isotopes** are atoms of the same element (same Z) with different numbers of neutrons. They have the same chemical properties and slightly different physical properties.

blocks.title: Relative atomic mass
blocks.md:
The **relative atomic mass** A_r is the weighted mean mass of an atom of the element compared with 1/12 of the mass of an atom of carbon-12.

**A_r = Σ(mass number × abundance %) ÷ 100.** A mass spectrometer ionises the atoms, accelerates them, deflects them in a magnetic field and detects them: each peak shows one isotope with its abundance.

blocks.caption: Sodium atom: 11 protons, 12 neutrons and electrons in shells 2, 8, 1.
blocks.alt: A nucleus with three concentric circles holding two, eight and one electrons.

blocks.title: Electron configuration
blocks.md:
Electrons occupy shells (n = 1, 2, 3…) made of subshells s (2 electrons, 1 orbital), p (6 electrons, 3 orbitals) and d (10 electrons, 5 orbitals). Fill in order of increasing energy: **1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p…** Each orbital holds two electrons of opposite spin; in a subshell, orbitals are filled singly first (Hund's rule).

Exceptions: Cr is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ and Cu is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ (half-full and full 3d are stable). Atoms form positive ions by losing the **4s** electrons before the 3d ones.

blocks.title: Ionisation energy
blocks.md: The **first ionisation energy** is the energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms: X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻ (kJ mol⁻¹). Successive ionisation energies increase, and a **large jump** shows the start of a new, inner shell: for example a big jump after the 2nd ionisation energy means 2 outer electrons (Group 2).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using the mass number (a whole number) instead of the weighted A_r (35.5 for chlorine).
- Writing Fe²⁺ as losing 3d electrons first: the 4s electrons go first.
- Saying isotopes differ in the number of protons or electrons.
- Forgetting that A_r has no units (it is relative).

blocks.title: Example 1 — Relative atomic mass
blocks.statement: Chlorine consists of 75 % ³⁵Cl and 25 % ³⁷Cl. Calculate A_r. Then give the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in ⁵⁶Fe³⁺.
steps: Fe has Z = 26, so 26 protons; neutrons = 56 − 26 = 30.
Fe³⁺ has lost three electrons: 26 − 3 = 23 electrons.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Configurations
blocks.statement: Write the electron configurations of Fe, Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺.
steps: Fe (Z = 26): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ 4s² (write 3d before 4s or after: both are accepted).
Fe³⁺ then loses one 3d electron: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁵ (a stable half-filled 3d subshell).

blocks.title: Atomic radius and shielding
blocks.md:
Across a period the nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell with similar shielding: the attraction increases and the **atomic radius decreases**. Down a group the outer electrons are in a higher shell, further from the nucleus and better shielded by the inner shells: the radius **increases** and the first ionisation energy **decreases**.

**Electronegativity** (the power of an atom to attract the bonding electrons in a covalent bond) increases across a period and decreases down a group; fluorine is the most electronegative.

blocks.title: First ionisation energy across period 3
blocks.md:
Generally the first ionisation energy **increases** across period 3 (greater nuclear charge, smaller radius). Two dips occur:

- **Mg → Al**: the 3p electron of Al is in a higher-energy subshell than the 3s electrons and is shielded by them, so is easier to remove.
- **P → S**: in S, the 3p⁴ configuration has a pair of electrons in one p orbital; the repulsion between them makes one easier to remove than the unpaired electrons of P (3p³).

blocks.caption: First ionisation energy across period 3 (kJ/mol): the dips are at Al and S.
blocks.alt: A bar chart of the first ionisation energies of sodium to argon with aluminium and sulfur lower than their predecessors.

blocks.title: Structure and melting point (period 3)
blocks.md:
- **Na, Mg, Al**: metallic lattices; melting points rise (98 °C, 650 °C, 660 °C) as the ion charge (1+, 2+, 3+) and the number of delocalised electrons increase and the ions become smaller.
- **Si**: giant covalent network: very high melting point (about 1410 °C).
- **P₄, S₈, Cl₂**: simple molecules held by weak London forces: low melting points (S₈ > P₄ > Cl₂, as the molecules are larger).
- **Ar**: single atoms, very low melting point.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Explaining ionisation energy trends only by 'more protons': also name the radius and shielding.
- Saying that the shielding increases across a period: it stays about the same.
- Explaining the melting points of molecular solids by the strength of covalent bonds: only the weak intermolecular forces are overcome.
- Forgetting that noble gases have no bonds between atoms apart from London forces.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Explaining a trend
blocks.statement: Explain why the first ionisation energy of Mg (738 kJ mol⁻¹) is greater than that of Na (496 kJ mol⁻¹), and why that of Al (578 kJ mol⁻¹) is lower than that of Mg.
steps: Na → Mg: the nuclear charge increases from 11+ to 12+ while the outer electron is in the same shell (3s), so the attraction is stronger: IE increases.
Mg → Al: Al's outer electron is a 3p electron, in a higher-energy subshell, shielded by the 3s electrons and by the filled inner shells.
The extra distance and shielding outweigh the greater nuclear charge, so Al needs less energy: 578 < 738.
blocks.answer: Mg → Al dip: the 3p electron is higher in energy and shielded

blocks.title: Example 2 — Predicting properties
blocks.statement: Predict which has the higher melting point, magnesium (2+, two delocalised electrons per atom) or sodium, and which of S₈ and Cl₂ has the higher melting point. Give reasons.
steps: Mg²⁺ has a higher charge and is smaller than Na⁺ and contributes two electrons: stronger metallic bonding, so Mg melts higher (650 °C against 98 °C).
S₈ and Cl₂ are simple molecules: melting needs only the London forces to be overcome.
The larger S₈ molecule has more electrons and stronger London forces, so S₈ has the higher melting point.

exercises.prompt: An element X in period 3 has the following successive ionisation energies (kJ mol⁻¹): 738, 1451, 7733, 10540, 13630.

parts.prompt: After which ionisation energy is the big jump (give the number of the ionisation energy: 1st, 2nd…).
parts.explanation: The jump from 1451 to 7733 occurs between the 2nd and 3rd.

parts.prompt: How many electrons are in the outer shell of X?
parts.explanation: The first two electrons are removed from the outer shell; the third comes from an inner shell.
Two outer electrons and three shells: magnesium.

parts.prompt: Explain why the 3rd ionisation energy is much larger than the 2nd.
parts.model: The third electron is removed from an inner shell (n = 2) which is closer to the nucleus and less shielded, so the attraction is much stronger and much more energy is needed.
parts.rubric: 1 mark: inner shell / closer to the nucleus; 1 mark: less shielding / stronger attraction.
parts.explanation: The third electron is removed from an inner shell (n = 2) which is closer to the nucleus and less shielded, so the attraction is much stronger and much more energy is needed.
